text.p: Wal-Mart Stores Inc's $1.2 billion move to acquire a controlling interest in Mexico retailer Cifra SA de CV should provide the largest U.S. retailer with an important source of long-term growth.

The deal gives Wal-Mart control of an additional 228 retail and restaurant outlets that were beyond the scope of its 6-year-old, 50-50 joint venture with Cifra. The joint venture had operated 145 stores and restaurants.
With $2.9 billion in sales in fiscal 1996 and net earnings of $257 million, Cifra is Mexico's largest retailer.

"Wal-Mart needed all the exposure to growth it can get," said Mark Husson, a research analyst with J.P. Morgan Securities. Wal-Mart needed to move aggressively with international expansion in order to maintain its historically high growth rate.

The move with Cifra is consistent with earlier analyses of Wal-Mart's international growth strategies. A March report from Salomon Brothers said the retailer has targeted expansion efforts in Latin America and Asia-Pacific rather than attempting to penetrate more mature and competitive markets in Western Europe and Japan.

The transaction, announced Tuesday, involves Cifra first paying a dividend of about $300 million to current shareholders. Then Wal-Mart will fold its stake in the joint venture into Cifra in exchange for between 38 and 39 percent of Cifra's Series A and B common stock.

Following approval of of the proposal by both companies' shareholders, Wal-Mart then will acquire an additional 12-to-13 percent of Cifra's Series A and B shares at a peso equivalent of between $1.89 and $2.03 per share through a $1.2 billion tender offer.
After the merger and tender offer, Wal-Mart expects to own a majority of the voting stock with an economic interest in post-merger Cifra of about 50 percent.

"They will control Cifra, rather than just participating as a partner," said Argus Research analyst David Toung. "The joint venture was successful, but Cifra had its own activities outside the joint venture that excluded Wal-Mart. This puts Wal-Mart in a position to benefit from those other activities."

Under the joint venture, Wal-Mart and Cifra operate 145 retail outlets and restaurants, but Cifra has another 228 coffee shops and discount department stores of its own outside the venture. Those will move into Wal-Mart control upon completion of the deal.

The deal will give Wal-Mart a stronger basis for future Latin American expansion. "Cifra has a wealth of experience in dealing with the economies of Latin America," said Wal-Mart spokesman Jay Fitzsimmons.

Analysts said the move probably will not have a significant effect on Wal-Mart's earnings projections for fiscal 1998. The First Call consensus estimate for Wal-Mart's fiscal 1998 earnings is $1.53 per share, a rise of 20 cents from 1997's actual earnings.
"We don't have information we need to make final adjustments to the earnings model," Husson said. "But it won't be more than a cent or part of a cent either way" for the year.
"Management says the deal is not dilutive, but it's hard to judge," Toung said. "We'll have to see as time goes on."
The deal will also allow Wal-Mart and Cifra to realize savings through consolidations of such activities as back-office operations and purchasing, Toung said.
Wal-Mart shares were up 3/8 late Tuesday at 30-7/8.
